[PREVIOUS AGENT OUTPUT]
# Returns Redesign: Turning a Cost Center Into a Second Sales Channel

*A working draft. I've built it as a hypothesis with the arithmetic exposed rather than a plan to be signed off — swap in your own numbers and the logic should still hold. Where I've made a judgement call, I've flagged the alternative so you can go a different way if your read of the business differs.*

---

## 0. The framing question worth sitting with first

The brief describes the problem as "returns cost too much." I'd gently suggest that's a symptom. Three separate things are happening, and they need separate treatments:

1. **Too many units come back** — a demand-side and content-side problem, not a policy problem.
2. **The ones that come back lose value while they wait** — a *velocity* problem. A garment sitting 21 days in an inspection queue isn't expensive because inspection is expensive; it's expensive because it missed its selling season.
3. **The ones that survive are sold into the wrong channel** — a *routing* problem. Liquidation at 20¢ on the dollar is a choice, usually made by default.

Notice that none of the three is solved by tightening the policy. Which is convenient, because the customer research is almost certainly right — and there's a stronger version of that insight worth exploiting: **if rivals are competing on return generosity, the retailer with the cheapest reverse cost per unit can afford to be the most generous and still win on margin.** That's the asymmetry I'd build toward. Loosen the promise where it's visible, tighten the economics where it isn't.

One counterintuitive move I'd put on the table early: **refund faster than you inspect.** Decouple the refund event from the physical receipt entirely for trusted customers. It improves the promise, it removes the customer-service cost of "where's my money," and — the part that matters — it frees you to route the physical unit on pure economics instead of on refund-authorization sequencing.

---

## 1. Illustrative baseline (replace with actuals)

I'll carry one arithmetic spine through the whole document so the recommendations are checkable.

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Units shipped / yr | 10.0M |
| Net revenue | $600M (AOV ≈ $60/unit) |
| Gross margin | 40% (COGS ≈ $36/unit) |
| Return rate | 28% → **2.8M returned units** |
| Outbound fulfilment cost/unit | $6.50 |
| **Reverse cost/unit** | **$8.00** (freight-in $4.20 · receive+inspect $2.10 · disposition handling $0.90 · care/admin $0.80) |
| Avg dwell, receipt → next shelf | 21 days |
| Blended net recovery (proceeds ÷ original retail) | **52%** ≈ $31.20/unit |
| Scrap rate | 12% |

**Leakage today**

| Component | Calculation | Annual |
|---|---|---|
| Reverse operating cost | 2.8M × $8.00 | **$22.4M** |
| Inventory value destruction | 2.8M × ($36 COGS − $31.20 proceeds) | **$13.4M** |
| Markdown contagion (late-returned stock cannibalising in-season full-price) | est. 0.5–0.8% of revenue | **$3–5M** |
| **Total identified leakage** | | **≈ $39–41M ≈ 6.5% of revenue** |

Two sensitivities worth knowing before anyone commits: **each $1.00 off reverse cost/unit ≈ $2.8M**, and **each 1 point of net recovery ≈ $1.7M**. Recovery is the bigger lever, and it's the one nobody is currently managing.

---

## 2. Return prevention — reduce returns without adding friction

The distinction to hold onto: *friction* prevention (harder to return) loses share. *Fit* prevention (fewer wrong purchases) gains it. Everything below is the second kind.

### 2.1 Fix the reason data before fixing anything else

You almost certainly can't see why goods come back. Coarse or free-text reason codes make every downstream decision guesswork.

- Capture **two** reason codes per unit: **customer-stated** (at initiation, guided, mutually exclusive, ~15–20 leaves) and **inspection-verified** (at grading). The *disagreement rate* between them is itself a diagnostic — where "changed my mind" turns out to be "defective," you have a vendor problem masquerading as a taste problem.
- Target: ≥95% of returns carrying a verified code within 90 days; disagreement rate tracked as a standing metric.

### 2.2 The prevention portfolio

| Driver (typical mix) | Intervention | Plausible reduction |
|---|---|---|
| **Fit / size (35–50% in apparel)** | Per-brand, per-body-type fit signal derived from *your own* keep/return history; "you kept M in this brand" personalisation; garment-measurement tables from actual specs, not vendor claims; size-confidence indicator on PDP | 15–25% of fit returns |
| **Expectation gap / "not as described" (15–20%)** | SKU-level content scorecard (on-model in ≥3 sizes, dimensional shot, material weight/GSM, scale reference, 15-sec video); mine returned-item photos and review images for what buyers were surprised by | 20–30% of this driver |
| **Bracketing (multi-size ordering)** | Don't penalise it — *out-compete* it. Instant fit-swap: exchange ships before the return arrives, so ordering one size beats ordering three. Optionally a small incentive (loyalty points, not a fee) for single-size orders | 10–20% of bracketed units |
| **Defect / quality** | Vendor PPM scorecard + verified-defect chargeback; pre-production and first-article inspection for repeat offenders | 30–50% of defect returns |
| **Transit damage** | Damage rate by SKU × carrier lane × pack spec; fragility tiering; right-sizing | 25–40% |
| **Wrong item picked** | Charge the cost back to the originating DC's own P&L. Pick accuracy improves quickly when the returns bill lands on the pick line | 40–60% |
| **Abuse / serial returns (1–3% of customers, 10–20% of loss)** | Behavioural scoring, not policy change. Differentiated *handling* —

# Critique: "Returns Redesign" Draft

## A. Blocking issue — the deliverable is roughly 25% complete

The request specified six mandatory components. The draft delivers two, and the second one is cut off mid-sentence ("Differentiated *handling* —").

| Required element | Status |
|---|---|
| Return prevention | Partial (table truncated, no roll-up) |
| Triage and grading | **Absent** |
| Refurbishment and secondary channels | **Absent** |
| Network design for reverse flows | **Absent** |
| Data feedback loop to merchandising | **Absent** |
| Quantified success measures | **Absent** (two sensitivities ≠ a measurement framework) |

Critically, the draft names *recovery rate* as "the bigger lever, and the one nobody is currently managing" — and then never addresses it. The document argues its way to the most important lever and stops. Similarly, the stated operational bottleneck in the brief (a manual inspection queue) is diagnosed as a velocity problem in §0 and then not touched again: no labour model, no automation option, no queue-flow design.

## B. Quantitative errors and internal inconsistencies

1. **Revenue base is inconsistent with unit volume.** 10.0M units shipped × $60 AOV = $600M *gross shipped value*, but the table labels $600M as "net revenue." With 2.8M returns, net revenue is ~$432M. This propagates: $39–41M leakage is **9.0–9.5% of net revenue**, not the stated 6.5%. Either the unit count, the AOV, or the revenue label is wrong. This is the headline number of the entire document.
2. **Reverse cost of $8.00 materially understates the true cost of a return.** It excludes: the sunk outbound pick/pack/ship ($6.50) and outbound freight, non-refunded payment processing fees (~1.5–2.5% of AOV), and any promotional discount already conceded. The *avoided* cost of preventing one return is roughly $8.00 + $6.50 + fees + retained margin on the sale that sticks — call it $20–25, not $8. Prevention ROI is therefore understated by ~3x, which distorts the lever ranking.
3. **"Recovery is the bigger lever" is asserted on non-comparable units.** $2.8M per $1.00 of cost vs. $1.7M per point of recovery tells you nothing until you state the *attainable range* of each. Do the work: cost compressible by ~$2.00–3.00 → $5.6–8.4M; recovery 52% → 62–68% → $17–27M. The conclusion is probably right; the argument as written doesn't support it.
4. **Additive sensitivities double-count.** "$1.00 off reverse cost = $2.8M" holds only at constant volume. If prevention cuts returns to 23%, that lever is worth $2.3M, not $2.8M. Levers must be modelled multiplicatively and sequenced, or the business case will overstate savings by 15–25%.
5. **Scrap rate 12% and blended recovery 52% are presented as independent parameters** — they aren't. Scrap is a disposition lane inside the recovery blend. As written, a reader cannot tell whether scrap loss is inside the $13.4M or additive to it. There is no disposition mix table, which is the analytic core of the recovery argument.
6. **Value destruction is measured against COGS, not against forgone margin.** 2.8M × ($36 − $31.20) captures cost erosion but not the opportunity: an A-grade unit resold in-season at full price recovers ~$60, not $36. The real prize is the gap between $31.20 and *achievable* recovery, which is never computed.
7. **Markdown contagion ($3–5M) is a pure assertion** ("est. 0.5–0.8% of revenue") yet is folded into the headline total. Either derive it from late-return re-entry timing vs. markdown cadence, or hold it below the line as an unvalidated upside. As is, it makes the whole baseline look invented.
8. **The 21-day dwell measures the wrong clock.** "Receipt → next shelf" omits customer hold time and inbound transit — typically another 10–20 days. The value-decay window is 30–45 days end-to-end. Understating it understates the velocity prize and misdirects effort to the inspection bench rather than to return initiation and freight.

## C. Analytical gaps within the sections that do exist

- **No roll-up of the prevention portfolio.** Per-driver reductions are given without driver base rates, so the reader cannot compute the answer to the only question that matters: does 28% become 26%, 23%, or 20%? By when? No investment cost, payback, owner, or sequencing accompanies any intervention — so it is a menu, not a plan.
- **Instant fit-swap is unpriced and possibly self-defeating.** Shipping the exchange before the return arrives *is* company-funded bracketing: you double the outbound cost and take inventory exposure to remove customer-funded bracketing. That may still win (higher conversion, fewer net units in the reverse chain), but the trade needs a per-transaction P&L, plus a rule for when it is offered (trust score, unit value, category).
- **Charging mispicks back to the DC P&L invites gaming** — under-reporting, disputed attribution, and DCs slowing throughput to protect an accuracy metric. Needs an audit mechanism and a paired throughput metric.
- **Vendor chargebacks assume leverage the retailer may not have.** For long-tail or marketplace vendors, a 30–50% defect reduction is unrealistic; the practical lever there is delisting or SKU-level content correction. Segment the vendor base before promising the number.

## D. Unsupported claims and risk blind spots

- **"Refund faster than you inspect" is the right instinct but the risk side is unexamined.** Missing: fraud/abuse cost estimate for the trusted cohort, cohort definition and size, revenue-recognition and returns-reserve implications, working-capital effect, and a fallback if abuse rises. A one-sided case on the single most contestable recommendation.
- **Differentiated handling for serial returners carries legal exposure that is not mentioned** — statutory withdrawal rights (e.g., UK/EU distance-selling rules), state consumer-protection statutes, and significant reputational precedent for silent blacklisting. Needs counsel sign-off and a disclosure design.
- **Direct contradiction left unreconciled:** §0 commits to "loosen the promise where it's visible," §2.2 introduces differentiated treatment of a customer segment. Explain how these coexist (e.g., loosen universally, differentiate only on *reverse handling economics*, never on refund eligibility) or the plan invites exactly the share loss the research warned about.
- **Regulatory and ESG exposure on scrap is absent.** A 12% scrap rate is now a compliance issue in several jurisdictions (French anti-waste law prohibiting destruction of unsold non-food goods; EU ESPR/EPR textile schemes), and destruction is increasingly a brand risk. Donation tax treatment and recycling partners are also unaddressed value.
- **The single largest freight lever is missing:** consolidated, label-free, bag-less drop-off at store/partner networks with cross-dock consolidation, which typically takes $1.50–2.50 out of the $4.20 freight line while *improving* the customer experience. Its absence is conspicuous.
- **"Keep it" / returnless refund thresholds** are absent, despite being the natural companion to decoupled refunds and the obvious answer for units where reverse cost + value loss exceeds recovery.
- **Category assumption is unstated.** The interventions are heavily apparel-specific ("garment," "GSM," body type) while the brief says "online retailer." State the assumption and flag how the design changes for electronics (serialisation, data wipe, warranty, repair) or furniture (freight-dominated economics).
- Several "typical mix" figures (fit 35–50%, abuse 1–3% of customers / 10–20% of loss) are presented as established facts without provenance. Label them as benchmarks with sources, or as assumptions to be validated in the first data pull.

## E. Framing and presentation

- The hedged preamble ("A working draft," "I'd gently suggest," "swap in your own numbers") consumes the highest-value real estate and undercuts authority. An executive audience needs the recommendation and the number in the first ten lines.
- The framing in §0 is genuinely strong — the three-way decomposition (volume / velocity / routing) and the "cheapest reverse cost can afford the most generous policy" asymmetry are the best ideas in the document. They deserve to be the spine of the whole plan; instead they are stated once and abandoned.
- Fabricating a full baseline is defensible only if paired with the specific data pulls needed to replace it. Add a one-page data request (reason-code extract, disposition-mix by lane, dwell-time distribution, recovery by lane and by days-since-receipt, return rate by SKU/vendor/customer cohort, repurchase rate of returners) with owners and a two-week deadline.

## F. What the next version must add

1. **Triage and grading:** decision at the point of *initiation*, not receipt — a disposition engine scoring each unit on predicted grade, unit value, category, days-of-season remaining, and reverse cost, routing to one of ~6 lanes (returnless keep-it / direct-to-restock cross-dock / light refurb / outlet / bulk liquidation / recycle-donate). Grading standard with photo evidence, audited sampling, target 24-hour touch-to-decision, and a stated in-house vs. 3PL vs. vision-assisted grading choice with cost per touch.
2. **Refurbishment and secondary channels:** per-lane P&L (proceeds, cost to serve, cannibalisation risk), channel mix target, brand-conflict guardrails, and the recovery-rate walk from 52% to target with contribution by lane.
3. **Network design:** node placement against return-origin density, drop-off/consolidation partner strategy, cross-dock direct-to-forward-stock for A-grade, single vs. multi-hub refurb centres, and a freight cost-per-unit walk.
4. **Merchandising feedback loop:** the specific decisions the loop changes (buy quantity, size curve, vendor scorecard, PDP content gate, SKU delisting rule), the cadence, the owner, and a hard rule such as "any SKU above X% return rate for two consecutive periods is content-remediated or exits the assortment."
5. **Measurement:** a KPI tree with baseline → 12-month target → owner, split into economics (reverse cost/unit, net recovery %, value-destroyed/unit, scrap %, total leakage as % of net revenue), velocity (initiation-to-resalable, % resold in-season), volume (return rate by cohort/driver), and **customer guardrails** (refund speed, returner NPS, 90-day repurchase rate of returners, share-of-wallet) with explicit stop-loss thresholds that halt cost initiatives if the promise degrades.
6. **Business case and phasing:** investment, payback, NPV, 0–90 day / quarters 2–4 / year 2 roadmap, and a risk register covering fraud, legal, vendor leverage, and channel conflict.

**Overall Assessment: MAJOR_REVISIONS**
[END QUALITY FEEDBACK]

| **Expectation gap / "not as described" (15–20%)** | SKU-level content scorecard (on-model in ≥3 sizes, dimensional shot, material weight/GSM, scale reference, 15-sec video); mine returned-item photos and review images for what buyers were surprised by | 20–30% of this driver |
| **Bracketing (multi-size ordering)** | Don't penalise it — *out-compete* it. Instant fit-swap: exchange ships before the return arrives, so ordering one size beats ordering three. Optionally a small incentive (loyalty points, not a fee) for single-size orders | 10–20% of bracketed units |
| **Defect / quality** | Vendor PPM scorecard + verified-defect chargeback; pre-production and first-article inspection for repeat offenders | 30–50% of defect returns |
| **Transit damage** | Damage rate by SKU × carrier lane × pack spec; fragility tiering; right-sizing | 25–40% |
| **Wrong item picked** | Charge the cost back to the originating DC's own P&L. Pick accuracy improves quickly when the returns bill lands on the pick line | 40–60% |
| **Abuse / serial returns (1–3% of customers, 10–20% of loss)** | Behavioural scoring, not policy change. Differentiated *handling* —

# Critique: "Returns Redesign" Draft

## A. Blocking issue — the deliverable is roughly 25% complete

The request specified six mandatory components. The draft delivers two, and the second one is cut off mid-sentence ("Differentiated *handling* —").

| Required element | Status |
|---|---|
| Return prevention | Partial (table truncated, no roll-up) |
| Triage and grading | **Absent** |
| Refurbishment and secondary channels | **Absent** |
| Network design for reverse flows | **Absent** |
| Data feedback loop to merchandising | **Absent** |
| Quantified success measures | **Absent** (two sensitivities ≠ a measurement framework) |

Critically, the draft names *recovery rate* as "the bigger lever, and the one nobody is currently managing" — and then never addresses it. The document argues its way to the most important lever and stops. Similarly, the stated operational bottleneck in the brief (a manual inspection queue) is diagnosed as a velocity problem in §0 and then not touched again: no labour model, no automation option, no queue-flow design.

## B. Quantitative errors and internal inconsistencies

1. **Revenue base is inconsistent with unit volume.** 10.0M units shipped × $60 AOV = $600M *gross shipped value*, but the table labels $600M as "net revenue." With 2.8M returns, net revenue is ~$432M. This propagates: $39–41M leakage is **9.0–9.5% of net revenue**, not the stated 6.5%. Either the unit count, the AOV, or the revenue label is wrong. This is the headline number of the entire document.
2. **Reverse cost of $8.00 materially understates the true cost of a return.** It excludes: the sunk outbound pick/pack/ship ($6.50) and outbound freight, non-refunded payment processing fees (~1.5–2.5% of AOV), and any promotional discount already conceded. The *avoided* cost of preventing one return is roughly $8.00 + $6.50 + fees + retained margin on the sale that sticks — call it $20–25, not $8. Prevention ROI is therefore understated by ~3x, which distorts the lever ranking.
3. **"Recovery is the bigger lever" is asserted on non-comparable units.** $2.8M per $1.00 of cost vs. $1.7M per point of recovery tells you nothing until you state the *attainable range* of each. Do the work: cost compressible by ~$2.00–3.00 → $5.6–8.4M; recovery 52% → 62–68% → $17–27M. The conclusion is probably right; the argument as written doesn't support it.
4. **Additive sensitivities double-count.** "$1.00 off reverse cost = $2.8M" holds only at constant volume. If prevention cuts returns to 23%, that lever is worth $2.3M, not $2.8M. Levers must be modelled multiplicatively and sequenced, or the business case will overstate savings by 15–25%.
5. **Scrap rate 12% and blended recovery 52% are presented as independent parameters** — they aren't. Scrap is a disposition lane inside the recovery blend. As written, a reader cannot tell whether scrap loss is inside the $13.4M or additive to it. There is no disposition mix table, which is the analytic core of the recovery argument.
6. **Value destruction is measured against COGS, not against forgone margin.** 2.8M × ($36 − $31.20) captures cost erosion but not the opportunity: an A-grade unit resold in-season at full price recovers ~$60, not $36. The real prize is the gap between $31.20 and *achievable* recovery, which is never computed.
7. **Markdown contagion ($3–5M) is a pure assertion** ("est. 0.5–0.8% of revenue") yet is folded into the headline total. Either derive it from late-return re-entry timing vs. markdown cadence, or hold it below the line as an unvalidated upside. As is, it makes the whole baseline look invented.
8. **The 21-day dwell measures the wrong clock.** "Receipt → next shelf" omits customer hold time and inbound transit — typically another 10–20 days. The value-decay window is 30–45 days end-to-end. Understating it understates the velocity prize and misdirects effort to the inspection bench rather than to return initiation and freight.

## C. Analytical gaps within the sections that do exist

- **No roll-up of the prevention portfolio.** Per-driver reductions are given without driver base rates, so the reader cannot compute the answer to the only question that matters: does 28% become 26%, 23%, or 20%? By when? No investment cost, payback, owner, or sequencing accompanies any intervention — so it is a menu, not a plan.
- **Instant fit-swap is unpriced and possibly self-defeating.** Shipping the exchange before the return arrives *is* company-funded bracketing: you double the outbound cost and take inventory exposure to remove customer-funded bracketing. That may still win (higher conversion, fewer net units in the reverse chain), but the trade needs a per-transaction P&L, plus a rule for when it is offered (trust score, unit value, category).
- **Charging mispicks back to the DC P&L invites gaming** — under-reporting, disputed attribution, and DCs slowing throughput to protect an accuracy metric. Needs an audit mechanism and a paired throughput metric.
- **Vendor chargebacks assume leverage the retailer may not have.** For long-tail or marketplace vendors, a 30–50% defect reduction is unrealistic; the practical lever there is delisting or SKU-level content correction. Segment the vendor base before promising the number.

## D. Unsupported claims and risk blind spots

- **"Refund faster than you inspect" is the right instinct but the risk side is unexamined.** Missing: fraud/abuse cost estimate for the trusted cohort, cohort definition and size, revenue-recognition and returns-reserve implications, working-capital effect, and a fallback if abuse rises. A one-sided case on the single most contestable recommendation.
- **Differentiated handling for serial returners carries legal exposure that is not mentioned** — statutory withdrawal rights (e.g., UK/EU distance-selling rules), state consumer-protection statutes, and significant reputational precedent for silent blacklisting. Needs counsel sign-off and a disclosure design.
- **Direct contradiction left unreconciled:** §0 commits to "loosen the promise where it's visible," §2.2 introduces differentiated treatment of a customer segment. Explain how these coexist (e.g., loosen universally, differentiate only on *reverse handling economics*, never on refund eligibility) or the plan invites exactly the share loss the research warned about.
- **Regulatory and ESG exposure on scrap is absent.** A 12% scrap rate is now a compliance issue in several jurisdictions (French anti-waste law prohibiting destruction of unsold non-food goods; EU ESPR/EPR textile schemes), and destruction is increasingly a brand risk. Donation tax treatment and recycling partners are also unaddressed value.
- **The single largest freight lever is missing:** consolidated, label-free, bag-less drop-off at store/partner networks with cross-dock consolidation, which typically takes $1.50–2.50 out of the $4.20 freight line while *improving* the customer experience. Its absence is conspicuous.
- **"Keep it" / returnless refund thresholds** are absent, despite being the natural companion to decoupled refunds and the obvious answer for units where reverse cost + value loss exceeds recovery.
- **Category assumption is unstated.** The interventions are heavily apparel-specific ("garment," "GSM," body type) while the brief says "online retailer." State the assumption and flag how the design changes for electronics (serialisation, data wipe, warranty, repair) or furniture (freight-dominated economics).
- Several "typical mix" figures (fit 35–50%, abuse 1–3% of customers / 10–20% of loss) are presented as established facts without provenance. Label them as benchmarks with sources, or as assumptions to be validated in the first data pull.

## E. Framing and presentation

- The hedged preamble ("A working draft," "I'd gently suggest," "swap in your own numbers") consumes the highest-value real estate and undercuts authority. An executive audience needs the recommendation and the number in the first ten lines.
- The framing in §0 is genuinely strong — the three-way decomposition (volume / velocity / routing) and the "cheapest reverse cost can afford the most generous policy" asymmetry are the best ideas in the document. They deserve to be the spine of the whole plan; instead they are stated once and abandoned.
- Fabricating a full baseline is defensible only if paired with the specific data pulls needed to replace it. Add a one-page data request (reason-code extract, disposition-mix by lane, dwell-time distribution, recovery by lane and by days-since-receipt, return rate by SKU/vendor/customer cohort, repurchase rate of returners) with owners and a two-week deadline.

## F. What the next version must add

1. **Triage and grading:** decision at the point of *initiation*, not receipt — a disposition engine scoring each unit on predicted grade, unit value, category, days-of-season remaining, and reverse cost, routing to one of ~6 lanes (returnless keep-it / direct-to-restock cross-dock / light refurb / outlet / bulk liquidation / recycle-donate). Grading standard with photo evidence, audited sampling, target 24-hour touch-to-decision, and a stated in-house vs. 3PL vs. vision-assisted grading choice with cost per touch.
2. **Refurbishment and secondary channels:** per-lane P&L (proceeds, cost to serve, cannibalisation risk), channel mix target, brand-conflict guardrails, and the recovery-rate walk from 52% to target with contribution by lane.
3. **Network design:** node placement against return-origin density, drop-off/consolidation partner strategy, cross-dock direct-to-forward-stock for A-grade, single vs. multi-hub refurb centres, and a freight cost-per-unit walk.
4. **Merchandising feedback loop:** the specific decisions the loop changes (buy quantity, size curve, vendor scorecard, PDP content gate, SKU delisting rule), the cadence, the owner, and a hard rule such as "any SKU above X% return rate for two consecutive periods is content-remediated or exits the assortment."
5. **Measurement:** a KPI tree with baseline → 12-month target → owner, split into economics (reverse cost/unit, net recovery %, value-destroyed/unit, scrap %, total leakage as % of net revenue), velocity (initiation-to-resalable, % resold in-season), volume (return rate by cohort/driver), and **customer guardrails** (refund speed, returner NPS, 90-day repurchase rate of returners, share-of-wallet) with explicit stop-loss thresholds that halt cost initiatives if the promise degrades.
6. **Business case and phasing:** investment, payback, NPV, 0–90 day / quarters 2–4 / year 2 roadmap, and a risk register covering fraud, legal, vendor leverage, and channel conflict.

**Overall Assessment: MAJOR_REVISIONS**
